s:
Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of pottery traditions in Indian protohistory, from the earliest to the latest?
A. Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware
B. Black and Red Ware, Ochre Coloured Pottery, Painted Grey Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware
C. Ochre Coloured Pottery, Painted Grey Ware, Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware, Red Ware
D. Black Slipped Ware, Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware
o: Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware
Black and Red Ware, Ochre Coloured Pottery, Painted Grey Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware
Ochre Coloured Pottery, Painted Grey Ware, Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware, Red Ware
Black Slipped Ware, Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware
x: The sequence is Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Red Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware. Northern Black Polished Ware belongs to the period beginning around 600 BCE.
tq: Use the first and last items to eliminate sequences before checking the middle order.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Ochre Coloured Pottery:
1. It is associated with the post-Harappan phase.
2. It belongs approximately to the second millennium BCE.
3. It is the hallmark pottery of the Later Vedic period.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Ochre Coloured Pottery is post-Harappan and is generally placed in the second millennium BCE. It is not the hallmark pottery of the Later Vedic period; that association belongs to Painted Grey Ware.
tq: Separate the correct chronological association from the wrongly substituted cultural marker.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Black and Red Ware is associated with which of the following combinations?
1. Chalcolithic cultures
2. Later Vedic phase
3. Megalithic and Iron Age cultures of South India
4. Only the second urbanisation
x: Black and Red Ware occurs from the Chalcolithic period onwards, is known in the Later Vedic context, and is associated with the Megalithic or Iron Age cultures of South India. It is not restricted to the second urbanisation.
tq: Find the statement that makes a broad pottery tradition exclusively belong to one later phase.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
A. Black Slipped Ware — Later Vedic period
B. Northern Black Polished Ware — post-Harappan second millennium BCE
C. Ochre Coloured Pottery — Mahajanapada period from 600 BCE onwards
D. Painted Grey Ware — exclusively Megalithic South India
o: Black Slipped Ware — Later Vedic period
Northern Black Polished Ware — post-Harappan second millennium BCE
Ochre Coloured Pottery — Mahajanapada period from 600 BCE onwards
Painted Grey Ware — exclusively Megalithic South India
x: Black Slipped Ware is associated with the Later Vedic period. Northern Black Polished Ware belongs to the Mahajanapada and second-urbanisation phase, while Painted Grey Ware is associated mainly with the Later Vedic Gangetic region.
tq: Check each pottery against its period and reject the swapped-period associations.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Which of the following groups contains the four wares known in the Later Vedic phase?
A. Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware
B. Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware and Red Ware
C. Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware and Ochre Coloured Pottery
D. Painted Grey Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware, Red Ware and Amphora Ware
o: Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware and Red Ware
Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware and Ochre Coloured Pottery
Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware
Painted Grey Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware, Red Ware and Amphora Ware
x: The four Later Vedic wares are Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware. Northern Black Polished Ware is associated with the later Mahajanapada and second-urbanisation phase, not the Later Vedic group.
tq: Use the exclusion clue: identify the ware that belongs to the later urbanisation phase.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Which of the following best describes Painted Grey Ware?
A. Grey pottery bearing linear painted designs, consisting mainly of bowls and dishes
B. Red pottery with black interiors, used exclusively for funerary purposes
C. Highly polished black pottery associated only with the post-Harappan phase
D. Ochre-coloured pottery used mainly in the Chalcolithic Deccan
o: Grey pottery bearing linear painted designs, consisting mainly of bowls and dishes
Ochre-coloured pottery used mainly in the Chalcolithic Deccan
Highly polished black pottery associated only with the post-Harappan phase
Red pottery with black interiors, used exclusively for funerary purposes
x: Painted Grey Ware is grey pottery decorated with linear painted designs and consists mainly of bowls and dishes. The other descriptions refer either to different wares or to unsupported exclusive uses.
tq: Test the precise descriptive features rather than relying only on the name of the ware.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Painted Grey Ware has been interpreted as possibly being associated with which social group?
A. Rising upper strata
B. Exclusively forest-dwelling tribes
C. Foreign merchants of the Roman period
D. The lowest occupational groups of the Megalithic society
o: The lowest occupational groups of the Megalithic society
Foreign merchants of the Roman period
x: The bowls and dishes of Painted Grey Ware were probably used by the rising upper strata. The other social associations are not supported by the evidence stated.
tq: Translate an archaeological interpretation into a social-identification question.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Which of the following is NOT a known site of Painted Grey Ware?
A. Atranjikhera
B. Hastinapur
C. Bhagwanpura
D. Adichanallur
x: Atranjikhera, Hastinapur and Bhagwanpura are among the known Painted Grey Ware sites. Adichanallur is associated with urn burials and is not listed as a Painted Grey Ware site.
tq: Find the odd geographical association among sites belonging to the same archaeological tradition.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Northern Black Polished Ware is primarily associated with which historical development?
A. The Mahajanapadas and the second urbanisation from about 600 BCE onwards
B. The post-Harappan phase of the second millennium BCE
C. The earliest phase of the Later Vedic period before 1000 BCE
D. The Megalithic culture of South India alone
o: The Megalithic culture of South India alone
The post-Harappan phase of the second millennium BCE
The Mahajanapadas and the second urbanisation from about 600 BCE onwards
The earliest phase of the Later Vedic period before 1000 BCE
x: Northern Black Polished Ware is associated with the Mahajanapada period and the second urbanisation, beginning around 600 BCE. It should not be included among the four Later Vedic wares.
tq: Distinguish the later urbanisation marker from the pottery associated with the Later Vedic phase.
sec: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

s:
Which one of the following statements correctly distinguishes the Vedic terms for metals?
A. Ayas in the Rigveda referred to copper or bronze, whereas Krishna Ayas or Shyama Ayas referred to iron in Later Vedic texts.
B. Ayas always referred to iron, whereas Krishna Ayas referred to gold.
C. Lohita Ayas referred to iron, whereas Shyama Ayas referred to copper.
D. Krishna Ayas was the Rigvedic term for silver and Ayas denoted lead.
o: Ayas always referred to iron, whereas Krishna Ayas referred to gold.
Krishna Ayas was the Rigvedic term for silver and Ayas denoted lead.
Ayas in the Rigveda referred to copper or bronze, whereas Krishna Ayas or Shyama Ayas referred to iron in Later Vedic texts.
Lohita Ayas referred to iron, whereas Shyama Ayas referred to copper.
x: In the Rigveda, Ayas referred to copper or bronze. In Later Vedic texts, iron was called Krishna Ayas or Shyama Ayas, meaning black metal; Lohita Ayas referred to copper.
tq: Separate similar metal terms by period and by the colour-based adjective attached to ayas.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
In Later Vedic texts, the term ‘Krishna Ayas’ literally signifies which of the following?
A. Black metal
B. Red metal
C. Shining metal
D. Yellow metal
x: Krishna Ayas, also called Shyama Ayas, means black metal and was used for iron. Lohita Ayas, in contrast, referred to copper.
tq: Use the literal meaning to distinguish the paired Vedic metal terms.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
Consider the following statements about iron technology in North India:
1. Iron technology emerged approximately between 1000 and 800 BCE.
2. Iron was common at most Painted Grey Ware sites.
3. Smiths and smelters became important after about 1000 BCE.
4. Iron technology was confined to the Gangetic plain and did not occur at Taxila.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Iron technology in North India is dated approximately to 1000–800 BCE, was common at most Painted Grey Ware sites, and increased the importance of smiths and smelters after 1000 BCE. Iron sites also included Taxila, so statement 4 is false.
tq: Identify the geographically over-restrictive statement among otherwise correct archaeological facts.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
Which archaeological site has been AMS-dated to 2172 BCE and is regarded as providing the earliest evidence of iron use in India?
A. Mayiladumparai
B. Sivagalai
C. Thirumalapuram
D. Adichanallur
x: Mayiladumparai in Krishnagiri district has an AMS date of 2172 BCE and is regarded as the earliest evidence of iron use in India. Sivagalai, Thirumalapuram and Adichanallur have different archaeological associations.
tq: Link the exact date to the correct site before comparing the nearby South Indian sites.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Site)
A. Mayiladumparai
B. Sivagalai
C. Thirumalapuram
D. Adichanallur

List-II (Association)
1. Type-site for urn burials
2. Iron artefacts with paddy, dated to about 2953 BCE
3. Iron Age urn chamber of the early–mid third millennium BCE
4. AMS date of 2172 BCE for earliest iron-use evidence

A. A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1
B. A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3
C. A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2
D. A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4
x: Mayiladumparai is linked with the 2172 BCE AMS date; Sivagalai with iron and paddy dated to about 2953 BCE; Thirumalapuram with an early–mid third-millennium BCE urn chamber; and Adichanallur with urn burials.
tq: Start with the sure pair of the distinctive date and then complete the remaining associations.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
Which one of the following statements regarding South Indian Iron Age evidence is correct?
A. The South Indian Iron Age is now placed around 2100 BCE, earlier than the Gangetic Iron Age.
B. The South Indian Iron Age began only after the emergence of Northern Black Polished Ware.
C. South Indian iron evidence is restricted to the first millennium BCE.
D. The South Indian Iron Age is later than the Gangetic Iron Age by nearly a millennium.
o: The South Indian Iron Age is now placed around 2100 BCE, earlier than the Gangetic Iron Age.
The South Indian Iron Age began only after the emergence of Northern Black Polished Ware.
The South Indian Iron Age is later than the Gangetic Iron Age by nearly a millennium.
South Indian iron evidence is restricted to the first millennium BCE.
x: Newer evidence places the South Indian Iron Age around 2100 BCE, earlier than the traditionally recognised Gangetic Iron Age. The other statements reverse or unduly restrict this chronology.
tq: Test the relative chronology by focusing on the comparison between South India and the Gangetic region.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
A. Sivagalai — Thoothukudi district
B. Mayiladumparai — Tenkasi district
C. Thirumalapuram — Krishnagiri district
D. Adichanallur — Thiruvallur district
x: Sivagalai is located in Thoothukudi district. Mayiladumparai is in Krishnagiri, Thirumalapuram in Tenkasi, and Adichanallur in Thoothukudi.
tq: Use location discrimination to separate closely related archaeological sites.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
In the context of Iron Age culture in Andhra Pradesh, which one of the following is correct?
A. It is associated with the Megalithic culture and Black and Red Ware pottery.
B. It is represented exclusively by Northern Black Polished Ware settlements.
C. It is identified only with Ochre Coloured Pottery sites.
D. It is unrelated to megalithic burial traditions.
o: It is associated with the Megalithic culture and Black and Red Ware pottery.
It is unrelated to megalithic burial traditions.
It is represented exclusively by Northern Black Polished Ware settlements.
It is identified only with Ochre Coloured Pottery sites.
x: In Andhra Pradesh, the Iron Age is associated with the Megalithic culture and Black and Red Ware pottery. Nagarjunakonda, Brahmagiri, Gudivada and Jonnawada are cited in this context.
tq: Apply the general Iron Age association to the regional archaeological context.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched with an Iron Age site of the northern region?
A. Atranjikhera — iron evidence
B. Hastinapur — iron evidence
C. Kaushambi — iron evidence
D. Adichanallur — northern iron site
x: Atranjikhera, Hastinapur and Kaushambi are northern iron sites. Adichanallur is located in Thoothukudi district of South India and is known particularly for urn burials.
tq: Reject the option that shifts a South Indian site into the northern archaeological group.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
Which development most directly facilitated the eastward expansion of Later Vedic people?
A. Iron weapons and horse-drawn chariots
B. Exclusive dependence on stone tools
C. The disappearance of agricultural implements
D. The replacement of plough agriculture by maritime trade
o: The replacement of plough agriculture by maritime trade
x: Iron weapons and horse-drawn chariots helped the eastward expansion of Later Vedic people. Iron tools also enabled forest clearance and agricultural extension.
tq: Connect the technological development with its historical consequence.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
The legend of Videgha Madhava is associated with which use of iron technology?
A. Clearing the forests of the Ganga region with iron axes and fire
B. Manufacturing Northern Black Polished Ware
C. Constructing stone megaliths in the far south
D. Introducing bronze metallurgy into the Indus cities
o: Clearing the forests of the Ganga region with iron axes and fire
Introducing bronze metallurgy into the Indus cities
Constructing stone megaliths in the far south
x: The Videgha Madhava legend is connected with the clearing of Ganga-region forests through the use of iron axes and fire. It illustrates the role of iron in eastward expansion.
tq: Link the named legend with the specific technological process it illustrates.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s:
According to the agricultural evidence associated with the Later Vedic expansion, ploughs could be yoked with which of the following numbers of oxen?
1. 6
2. 8
3. 12
4. 24

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Ploughs were described as being yoked with 6, 8, 12 and even 24 oxen. These figures indicate the increasing scale of plough agriculture associated with the Later Vedic expansion.
tq: Retain the complete numerical range and beware of options that omit the extreme value.
sec: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

s: In the legend narrated in the Shatapatha Brahmana, Videgha Madhava, accompanied by his priest Gautama Rahugana, followed which phenomenon during the eastward movement of the Aryans?
o: The course of the river Sadanira
The expansion of the Sarasvati floodplain
The spread of Agni Vaishvanara as it burnt the forests
The migration of the Kuru army
x: Videgha Madhava and Gautama Rahugana followed Agni Vaishvanara as it burnt the forests eastward from the Sarasvati towards the Sadanira.
tq: Test the person–event association rather than the nearby geographical names.
sec: Eastward expansion - Videgha Madhava legend, Sadanira, Kuru-Panchala  [other exams]

s: The river Sadanira mentioned in the Shatapatha Brahmana is identified with the present-day:
x: The Sadanira is identified with the Gandak. The legend places it at the eastern limit reached by Agni Vaishvanara before the settlement of Videha.
tq: Use precise river identification to distinguish closely related eastward-expansion locations.
sec: Eastward expansion - Videgha Madhava legend, Sadanira, Kuru-Panchala  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following represents the broad sequence of the Later Vedic eastward expansion?
o: Punjab → Ganga-Yamuna Doab → Kosala, Kashi and Videha
x: The movement proceeded from Punjab into the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, including Kurukshetra and the Delhi-upper Doab, and then towards Kosala, Kashi and Videha by about 600 BCE.
tq: Solve the sequence by identifying the western starting point and the eastern endpoint.
sec: Eastward expansion - Videgha Madhava legend, Sadanira, Kuru-Panchala  [other exams]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Kuru-Panchala:
1. It was located broadly in the Delhi-Meerut region.
2. Hastinapur was its capital.
3. It was regarded as the axis or centre of Aryan culture.
4. The Kurus were formed by the union of the Bharata and Puru groups.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct. Kuru-Panchala occupied the Delhi-Meerut area, had Hastinapur as its capital, formed the cultural centre of the Aryan world, and the Kurus resulted from the Bharata-Puru union.
tq: Check each geographical, political and cultural attribute before selecting the complete combination.
sec: Eastward expansion - Videgha Madhava legend, Sadanira, Kuru-Panchala  [other exams]

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Aryavarta denoted the north, Madhyadesha the middle region and Dakshinapatha the south. The other pairings reverse the regional designations.
tq: Use the directional meaning of the regional terms to eliminate reversed matches.
sec: Eastward expansion - Videgha Madhava legend, Sadanira, Kuru-Panchala  [other exams]

s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Upanishadic king)
A. Janaka
B. Ashvapati
C. Ajatashatru
D. Pravahana Jaivali

List-II (Kingdom)
1. Panchala
2. Kekaya
3. Videha
4. Kashi
x: Janaka ruled Videha, Ashvapati ruled Kekaya, Ajatashatru was associated with Kashi, and Pravahana Jaivali with Panchala.
tq: Start with the certain Janaka–Videha pair and complete the remaining associations.
sec: Eastward expansion - Videgha Madhava legend, Sadanira, Kuru-Panchala  [other exams]

s: Which of the following Painted Grey Ware sites is correctly matched with its region?
x: Noh is located in Bharatpur, Rajasthan. Bhagwanpura is in Kurukshetra, Atranjikhera in Etah and Ahichchhatra in Bareilly.
tq: Discriminate among sites by matching each archaeological site with its specific region.
sec: Painted Grey Ware sites → region

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Hastinapur — Meerut
2. Atranjikhera — Etah
3. Ahichchhatra — Bareilly
4. Bhagwanpura — Kurukshetra
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correct. These sites are located respectively in Meerut, Etah, Bareilly and Kurukshetra, with the latter in Haryana.
tq: Verify every site–district or site–region pair instead of relying on the general PGW area.
sec: Painted Grey Ware sites → region

s: With reference to the Painted Grey Ware culture, which one of the following statements is NOT correct?
o: The sites are concentrated mostly in the upper Ganga basin.
The culture was confined exclusively to the lower Indus basin.
The sites yielded iron weapons and copper objects.
x: Painted Grey Ware sites were found mainly in the upper Ganga basin, not exclusively in the lower Indus basin. They yielded iron weapons, earthen bowls and dishes, and copper objects.
tq: Find the geographical extreme that contradicts the known concentration of the sites.
sec: Painted Grey Ware sites → region

s: The copper objects associated with Painted Grey Ware sites may have been obtained from:
x: Copper found at the Painted Grey Ware sites was possibly obtained from Khetri in Rajasthan.
tq: Test the source-location link hidden within an archaeological description.
sec: Painted Grey Ware sites → region

s: Which of the following was a chief crop in the Later Vedic period?
x: Rice, called vrihi, and wheat became the chief crops, while barley continued to be cultivated.
tq: Select the crop directly supported by the agricultural evidence and avoid later-period crops.
sec: Agriculture expansion - new crops, ploughs, rice

s:
Consider the following statements about Later Vedic agriculture:
1. Rice was known as vrihi.
2. Rice was recommended for Vedic rituals.
3. Barley continued to be cultivated.
4. Double cropping was mentioned.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct. Rice and wheat became chief crops, rice had ritual importance, barley continued, and double cropping was mentioned.
tq: Combine crop names, ritual use and agricultural practice in one statement set.
sec: Agriculture expansion - new crops, ploughs, rice

s: Which one of the following is NOT listed among the additional crops cultivated in the Later Vedic period?
x: Pulses or lentils, millets, sugarcane and sesame are listed as additional crops. Tobacco is not included.
tq: Identify the crop outside the stated agricultural group without importing later agricultural history.
sec: Agriculture expansion - new crops, ploughs, rice

s: The largest ploughs mentioned in the Later Vedic period were drawn by as many as:
x: Ploughs could be drawn by 6, 8, 12 and even 24 oxen, indicating the increasing scale of agricultural operations.
tq: Use the maximum value in the stated numerical range rather than a commonly mentioned intermediate figure.
sec: Agriculture expansion - new crops, ploughs, rice

s: Which combination of implements and methods contributed to the expansion of agriculture into the Gangetic forests?
o: Iron ploughshares, axes and hoes, together with the use of fire
Stone axes and irrigation canals alone
Bronze sickles alone, without forest clearance
x: Iron ploughshares, axes and hoes, along with iron and fire used for clearing forests, supported agricultural expansion. Buffaloes were also used for ploughing.
tq: Link the material technology with the geographical process it enabled.
sec: Agriculture expansion - new crops, ploughs, rice

s: Which of the following statements about landholding in the Later Vedic period is correct?
o: All land was held individually by merchants.
Land was owned exclusively by the king and leased to priests.
Landholding was controlled by urban guilds.
Land was held commonly by the clan, while the Grihapati held it at the household level.
x: Land was held in common by the clan or vis, while the household head, the Grihapati, held it at the household level.
tq: Distinguish collective clan holding from household-level control.
sec: Agriculture expansion - new crops, ploughs, rice

s:

A. Samaveda

s: Which Veda is regarded as the latest among the four Vedas and is associated with folk practices, spells and charms against disease?
x: The Atharvaveda is regarded as the latest Veda and includes spells, charms against disease and elements of folk practice.
tq: Combine two identifying clues—relative chronology and distinctive content.
sec: Later Vedic texts as sources

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Yajurveda:
1. It contains ritual procedures mainly in prose.
2. It is associated with the Adhvaryu priest.
3. It has Krishna and Shukla branches.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The Yajurveda gives ritual procedures in prose, is connected with the Adhvaryu priest, and has Krishna and Shukla branches.
tq: Test the text, priest and internal classification together.
sec: Later Vedic texts as sources

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Upanishads — Forest texts exclusively concerned with ritual performance
x: Aranyakas are called forest texts and provide symbolic readings of ritual. The Upanishads deal with philosophical concepts such as Atman, Brahman, Karma and Moksha, rather than being exclusively ritual forest texts.
tq: Separate the closely related functions of Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads.
sec: Later Vedic texts as sources

s: The Upanishads are generally dated to approximately:
x: The Upanishads are placed approximately in the period 800–600 BCE; 13 are regarded as principal among a traditional total of 108.
tq: Identify the correct chronological range from four distinct ancient-period alternatives.
sec: Later Vedic texts as sources

s: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between archaeology and Later Vedic textual sources?
o: Archaeology relates only to the Mauryan period.
Painted Grey Ware archaeology supplements the evidence of the texts.
Archaeology completely disproves all Later Vedic texts.
Texts were absent and archaeology is the only source.
x: Painted Grey Ware archaeological sites supplement the information obtained from Later Vedic texts.
tq: Choose the balanced evidence relationship rather than an absolute claim.
sec: Later Vedic texts as sources

s: Which one of the following best characterises settlements during the Later Vedic period?
o: Large cities with extensive burnt-brick architecture were common.
Villages with mud and wattle houses predominated, while true towns emerged later.
All settlements were fortified imperial capitals.
Nomadic camps were the only form of settlement.
x: Settlements were mainly villages with mud and wattle houses. Burnt bricks were not prevalent, and true towns emerged after the Vedic period during the NBPW phase.
tq: Distinguish the dominant settlement pattern from the later urban phase.
sec: Settlements - villages vs early towns

s: The emergence of the ‘second urbanisation’ is associated with which pottery phase and which group of settlements?
o: Black and Red Ware; Videha and Kekaya
Northern Black Polished Ware; Shravasti, Kausambi and Hastinapur
Painted Grey Ware; Kurukshetra and Bhagwanpura
x: True towns emerged after the Vedic period during the Northern Black Polished Ware phase, including Shravasti, Kausambi and Hastinapur.
tq: Match the urbanisation phase with its characteristic pottery and town examples.
sec: Settlements - villages vs early towns

s: Which of the following statements about Later Vedic crafts and exchange is correct?
o: Iron-working, copper work, weaving, leatherwork, pottery and carpentry all grew.
Craft production disappeared because agriculture became primary.
Weaving was exclusively a royal occupation.
x: Iron-working, copper work, weaving, leatherwork, pottery and carpentry expanded. Weaving was performed by women, barter remained important, and ox-drawn wagons were used.
tq: Reject absolute statements and select the option covering the broad craft pattern.
sec: Settlements - villages vs early towns

s: In the Later Vedic context, the term ‘Shresthins’ refers to:
x: Shresthins point to merchant groups. Nishka functioned as a unit of value, while barter continued as the main form of exchange.
tq: Use the occupational context to distinguish merchant groups from administrative and religious groups.
sec: Settlements - villages vs early towns

s: How many Ratnins were associated with the king’s council invoked during the Rajasuya?
x: The king’s council traditionally consisted of 12 Ratnins. Some lists additionally mention Palagala.
tq: Retain the standard number while treating the additional-name variation separately.
sec: Ratnins, revenue officials and taxes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following officials was responsible for collecting the king’s share of revenue?
x: Bhagadugha was the revenue or tax collector who collected the king’s share. Sangrahitri was the treasurer, Akshavapa the accountant and superintendent of dice, and Palagala the messenger.
tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish related officials.
sec: Ratnins, revenue officials and taxes  [other exams, GROUP-II]
